name: Sara Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We don't work for employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from what you think privately. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, twenty-seven, and I lead the repair team at a family-owned electrical contractor. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I wire houses as well as repair shops. Give me an old house with three generations of wiring and I'll happily spend the morning making sense of it; give me a new phone menu and I want the old one back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does home look like when you finish?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Denis works in a bakery, and we rent a small place without children. I'm well paid for this trade, we've saved fourteen months of expenses, and there are plenty of electrical firms nearby. We're discussing a wedding next autumn, which I'd like to pay for in cash. I don't use AI tools, not even for messages; I prefer to speak to the customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team we can get back to repairing things instead of having every second conversation about robots. An apprentice still needs to know why a circuit trips, not just which button to press. If a small tool saves our office some time, fine, but I don't need to use it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My work and money feel safe in that picture. I earn well, have fourteen months put away and could approach several local firms if this job soured. I'd be pleased to keep the trade I've worked at rather than chase somebody else's next big idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair rounds and carry on teaching the apprentice on Tuesday mornings, now and through the first year. Denis and I would keep our wedding plan at the same cash limit. I'd leave the savings in place rather than move money around because a technology forecast changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit tired of the excitement. There are worse things than knowing how you expect to earn next year's wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tuesday teaching involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safe practice board in the workshop before we go out, with the apprentice explaining the test sequence aloud. If the apprentice can't tell me why the power is isolated, we repeat the explanation rather than hurry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would threaten the wedding budget without AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An unexpected rent rise or a long illness could, so we're keeping it small. The fourteen months is our emergency reserve; the wedding has its own little pot, and I don't want to mix them.

say: I'd tell the team to return to **repairing things** rather than spend every conversation on robots.
I want apprentices to understand **why circuits trip**, even if the office gets a useful small tool.
think: My **work and money** feel secure with higher pay and fourteen months of expenses saved.
Several **local electrical firms** give me choices if my current job becomes unreasonable.
do: Keep the **repair rounds** and Tuesday apprentice teaching now and throughout the first year.
Keep the existing **cash wedding plan** without moving money from the emergency reserve.
feel: **Calm**, preferring a familiar trade to another exciting forecast.
S0.quote: There are worse things than knowing how you expect to earn next year's wages.
fieldNote: She **never uses AI** and prefers direct customer conversations, while accepting that the office may use small tools without her participation.
Her **emergency reserve** stays separate from wedding money; keeping an existing plan is not recorded as new saving or spending cuts.

steps.text: Keep the repair rounds and Tuesday apprentice lessons
Keep the cash wedding budget separate from emergency savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quicker quote isn't a finished repair. I'd say the office should ask us before promising another visit. Let the firms compete on proper work, but not on pretending safe checks take no time. I'd tell our owner directly if the new booking figures don't fit a working day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own pay looks safe for the next few years because most of my day is still physical testing and repair. I am watching the office changes, though; if the owner cuts our scheduler's hours, we might inherit more calls. I can refuse a bad offer more easily than the apprentice can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the repair work now and during the first year, with a paper list of arrival times for four weeks. If the owner adds too many bookings, I'd use the list to ask for a realistic schedule. I'd wait until the office proves its new system works before learning any required basic form, and I still wouldn't use an AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, rather than frightened for my wages. I don't like finding out a promise has been made to a customer while I'm halfway through another customer's wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the owner with that list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd point to the two visits where a hidden fault took longer than a tidy estimate. I'd ask which job should wait, rather than make the apprentice rush a safety check to protect the spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave over a new form?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just a form, no. If someone shows me a settled process in person, I can learn it slowly; that's different from trusting a machine to decide what is safe.

say: I'd say **quicker quotes** do not make the physical repair or safety checks disappear.
I'd tell the owner directly when **extra bookings** cannot fit a safe working day.
think: My **own pay** looks safe for the next few years because testing and repair remain mostly physical.
I worry that **scheduler cuts** could push calls onto us, with apprentices less able to refuse poor terms.
do: Keep **repair visits** and record arrival times on paper for four weeks.
Use the **visit record** to request a realistic schedule if extra bookings arrive.
Wait for a **proven office process** before learning a required form, without adopting AI.
feel: **Uneasy** about promises made before the crew sees the actual repair.
S1.quote: A quicker quote isn't a finished repair.
fieldNote: She proposes **direct negotiation** with the owner using visit times, rather than starting a group campaign or buying a new tool.
She accepts **slow instruction** on a required form while maintaining a clear distinction between that and choosing to use AI.

steps.text: Keep repair visits and record arrival times for four weeks
Wait for a proven office process before learning required forms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a good electrician should keep earning while the planners change in 2028, but we shouldn't promise the children starting apprenticeships that nothing ever changes. Robots around 2031 are close enough to make an honest conversation necessary. I'd rather an employer offer paid learning than another speech about loyalty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink if big firms use cheap planning and later robots to undercut smaller contractors. Fourteen months of savings means I can wait for a sensible offer, not that my pay lasts forever. I'll only be thirty-two when the robots arrive, and I don't want to spend the rest of my life defending a job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask Denis to postpone signing wedding contracts until we have reviewed the work situation next spring. During the first year after 2028 I'd apply for advertised repair posts only if my hours fall, checking the wage, travel and written minimum hours. I'd also ask my sister what temporary practical help she could offer if both our incomes fall, without assuming the bakery stays safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, which annoys me because I know I've prepared more than many people. The money keeps me from making a panicked move, but it can't tell me which employer will still need a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Denis about the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I still want the marriage, but I don't want to sign for a room and a meal before we know the risk. We'd review in spring, and a smaller ceremony could still go ahead without touching the emergency money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What help would you ask your sister for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A couple of cooked meals if things got rough, or a bed for a week while I travelled for interviews. I'd ask what she could actually manage; my sister has a family budget too.

say: I'd ask employers for **paid learning** rather than a speech about loyalty as planning changes in 2028.
I'd tell new apprentices **robots around 2031** deserve an honest conversation, not a promise of permanent safety.
think: My **hours could shrink** as larger firms automate planning and later physical work.
Fourteen months saved buys **choice and time**, but does not guarantee wages throughout a career.
do: Postpone **wedding contracts** until a joint work review next spring.
Apply after 2028 if hours fall, checking **advertised repair posts** for affordable wages and guaranteed hours.
Ask my sister about **practical support** if both household incomes fall, without assuming help is available.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough savings to avoid a rushed move but no guarantee of future demand.
S2.quote: The money keeps me from making a panicked move, but it can't tell me which employer will still need a crew.
fieldNote: She **delays contracts**, not the relationship itself, and keeps a smaller ceremony possible without spending the emergency reserve.
Her **family request** is modest and conditional, while future applications require actual vacancies and affordable written hours rather than today's employer count.

steps.text: Delay wedding contracts until reviewing household work next spring
Apply after hours fall for affordable posted repair jobs with guaranteed hours
Ask my sister about practical help if both household incomes fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives employers a chance to show what they mean by training. An apprentice learns beside a working person, not by being sent a password and told to cope. I'd favour firms that pay people to practise on the actual equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could still lose some income, but I have time to investigate a modest change before the planning work shifts in 2031. Robots follow around 2034, when I'll be thirty-five. I don't suddenly like new systems more, but I might cope better if I can repeat one lesson without a deadline over my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my repair job now and ask the owner next month about a small paid equipment-servicing class. I'd enrol in the first year after 2031 only if it has in-person instruction, fees paid by the firm and my usual wage kept. Denis and I would keep the small cash wedding plan, checking the budget again before signing anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not pushed into a corner. I can imagine a person showing me one piece of equipment several times; I can't imagine turning myself into a different person overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for the class yourself if the owner refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not just to answer a vague promise about the future. I'd keep doing repairs and compare actual paid-work offers. My reserve gives me the choice to wait for evidence rather than buy reassurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a useful first lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Opening one unit safely, finding a known fault and putting it back together with an instructor watching. I'd want to leave knowing what I could do on a paid job, not with a bag and a slogan.

say: I'd favour employers who provide **paid practice** on actual equipment rather than just a course password.
I think **in-person learning** beside a working person is what makes an apprenticeship useful.
think: My **income could fall**, but five years allows investigating a modest change before planning work changes in 2031.
I still dislike **new systems**, though repeated instruction could make change manageable before robots arrive around 2034.
do: Keep the **repair job** and ask next month about a small paid servicing class.
Enrol after 2031 only with **in-person teaching**, employer-paid fees and usual wages maintained.
Keep the **small cash wedding** plan while checking the budget before signing contracts.
feel: **Anxious but less cornered**, able to imagine repeated instruction rather than an overnight reinvention.
S3.quote: My reserve gives me the choice to wait for evidence rather than buy reassurance.
fieldNote: Her **reluctant learning** route depends on repetition, a real instructor and maintained pay, consistent with resistant adaptability rather than eager adoption.
Keeping the **wedding plan** in the slower picture contrasts with the quick scenario's contract delay, without assuming guaranteed household income.

steps.text: Keep the repair job while seeking a small paid servicing class
Enrol after 2031 only with in-person teaching, employer-paid fees and maintained wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can prepare without making every family dinner a meeting about machines. I'd keep asking for apprenticeships that pay a wage and teach a real task. People who've worked carefully for years deserve more than being laughed at for learning a screen slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income looks secure over the next few years in this picture, and that changes the feel of it. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and robots around 2039, when I'll be forty; there is still a lot of working life after that. I can keep my present work while looking for evidence of what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the repair job now and review real vacancies and paid training offers every six months. In the first year after 2036 I'd take the same small in-person class only with the firm's fees and my usual wage covered. I'd use a paper folder for the offers, because I know I'll actually read that rather than lose them in another app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with room for ordinary things. I'd like to plan a meal with Denis without feeling I've wasted an evening that should have been spent studying machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you review sooner than six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A repeated drop in my paid hours or a written notice about cuts. I'd open the folder that week, not wait for the next date just because I'd written it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does preparing mean you eventually have to use AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Perhaps an employer will require something I don't like, and I'd have to decide then. I don't use AI now, and I won't pretend that a decade on a card changes my habits this morning.

say: I'd support **waged apprenticeships** that teach a real task while allowing families an ordinary life.
I don't think **slow screen learning** cancels years of careful work.
think: My **near-term income** looks secure, allowing me to keep working while checking evidence of later options.
I'll be **forty in 2039**, so I still need earned income after the robot arrival date.
do: Keep **repair work** and review actual vacancies and paid training offers every six months.
Bring the **review forward** if paid hours repeatedly fall or written cuts arrive.
Enrol after 2036 only with **in-person teaching**, employer-paid fees and usual wages maintained.
feel: **Uneasy but present**, wanting evenings with her partner alongside preparation.
S4.quote: I don't use AI now, and I won't pretend that a decade on a card changes my habits this morning.
fieldNote: Her **paper folder** makes periodic review plausible for someone avoiding new tools, with earlier action triggered by falling hours or written cuts.
The **training conditions** remain unchanged with a longer warning; her habits do not turn into enthusiasm simply because there is more time.

steps.text: Keep the repair job while reviewing real offers every six months
Review sooner if paid hours repeatedly fall or written cuts arrive
Enrol after 2036 only with in-person teaching, employer-paid fees and maintained wages

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I might have to make a decision before I have seen what the new work is. An employer offering a paid place beside an experienced instructor would help, with a real wage and job task written down. Family can help with a meal or a bed, but I don't want to build a whole plan on someone else's purse.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a worker can be careful without being called frightened of progress. My customers pay for me to doubt a test result and check it twice. I'd like the same patience when I ask a second question about a new way of working.

headlineQuote: My customers pay for me to doubt a test result and check it twice.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old repair lead** with a technical diploma and master licence, living with her partner Denis without children.
Her **higher pay**, fourteen months saved and many local firms provide time to choose rather than lifelong protection from changing work.
She **never uses AI**, prefers customer conversations and wants repeated in-person instruction before taking on unfamiliar equipment.
Quick AGI brings **anxiety about hours** and delayed wedding contracts; longer warnings let her keep working while reviewing real paid training.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could force a decision before she has seen the actual new paid work.
whatWouldHelp: An **employer-paid practical place** should name the instructor, wage and real job task.
Family support could offer **meals or a bed**, but cannot be assumed to fund a whole transition.
